# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review of the two-year follow-up report

**Bottom line:** This report is a serious attempt to settle the open questions in this exchange, and it largely succeeds:
- It finds a smaller but lasting per-hour gain in discretionary work under strong measurement.
- It finds clear failure in coverage-bound work.
- It shows the meta-analysis's no-decay claim rested on weak studies.

Three problems undercut parts of it:
- **The system-log hours measure seems to conflict with the meeting data.** If log time excludes meetings, the figures don't reconcile, and this affects both the hours correction and the mediation result.
- **Two control offices changed their own practices partway through.** That contaminates the comparison, and could explain some of the apparent "fading".
- **The summary claims more than the body supports.** It mixes hours measures and overstates the mediation finding.

## Checks

These figures reconcile:
- **Varden at 24 months.** 0.966 / 0.88 = +9.8% using timesheets, and 0.966 / 0.89 = +8.5% using logs.
- **Halden continuers.** 34.9 / 40.3 = −13.4%, and 96.8 / 86.6 = +11.8%.
- **Mediation shares.** 47 + 18 + 35 = 100.
- **Counter arm.** A per-employee fall of 11.4% implies about 13% more staff to restore output (1 / 0.886). That roughly matches the "12% more staff".

Two items need explanation:
- **Cost per contact.** 12% more staff at unchanged pay should raise cost per contact by about 12% if contacts return to baseline. The reported 9% only follows if labour is about 75% of total cost. State the assumption.
- **Size of the decline.** Section 5 says the gain "declined by about a quarter". On the like-for-like timesheet measure, 12.5% → 9.8% is about a fifth (about 21% on the log scale). "About a quarter" is closer to the 12.5% → 8.5% comparison, which mixes measures.

## Main issues

**1. The system-log hours may not measure the same thing as timesheets.**

The paper says logs record time "working on cases". A case-management system would not normally record time in meetings. If that holds, the figures don't fit together:
- At baseline, treated staff logged about 37.9 timesheet hours, including about 7.4 hours of meetings. That leaves about 30.5 hours of non-meeting time.
- At 24 months, timesheets are down about 12% (to roughly 33.4 hours). Meetings are down to 3.9 hours. That leaves about 29.5 hours of non-meeting time.
- Case time therefore fell by only about 3%, not 11%. Control offices' meeting time was flat, so the difference-in-differences comparison doesn't remove the gap.

So either log time includes something beyond case work, or the hours figures are inconsistent.

This matters in two ways:
- **The hours comparison.** "Log data show slightly more work than timesheets" compares percentage changes in what may be two different quantities.
- **The mediation result.** If the outcome is output per hour of case work, cutting meetings shouldn't raise it mechanically. Freed meeting time would add case hours to the denominator. A meetings effect on that outcome would then have to work through fewer interruptions or better focus, which is a different and more interesting mechanism than "removing low-value time".

The paper should define exactly what log time captures. It should also report baseline log hours alongside timesheet hours.

**2. The meeting audit in two control offices contaminates the comparison.**
- In month 15, two of the seven control offices cut meetings and saw output per hour rise 4.1%. Averaged across all seven control offices, that would raise the control trend by roughly 1 point from month 15 onward.
- That narrows the gap between treated and control offices. So part of the "decline" from 12.5% to 9.8% may come from controls improving, not from treated offices fading.
- The audit may itself have been prompted by the trial, since control staff knew it was running.

The paper treats this as a side observation. It is actually a threat to the 24-month estimate and to the decay interpretation. The authors should report the estimates with those two offices excluded, or with their post-audit months excluded.

**3. The decline itself is not tested.** The 9-month and 24-month intervals overlap heavily (+6.9 to +18.4 versus +4.6 to +15.2). The body hedges appropriately: "consistent with some fading". The summary states flatly that the gain "has declined". A within-office test of the change, adjusted for the contamination above, is needed before calling it a decline.

**4. The summary overstates the mediation result.**
- **"Confirms" is too strong.** The Limitations section itself says mediation in a cluster trial depends on the assumption of no unmeasured confounding. Offices that cut meetings most may differ in management quality, which affects output through other routes. "Is consistent with" fits better.
- **"Larger sample of office-months" overstates the sample.** Office-months are not independent, and there are still only 14 offices. An interval of 28–66% looks narrow for that, so the method behind it should be reported.
- **This is not an independent replication.** The same seven treated offices generated the hypothesis and then supplied the test. Registering it still helps, but the test covers a new time period, not new units.
- **The shares depend on model ordering.** Fewer meetings may reduce fatigue. The 47/18 split depends on how the model orders the two mediators, so it should be reported with a sensitivity analysis.

**5. The summary mixes hours measures.** "Fell from 12.5% … to 8.5% … measured with system log data" compares a timesheet figure with a log figure. Section 3 does this correctly by setting 12.5% beside 9.8%. The summary should do the same.

## Halden subset

- **"Upper bound" is the wrong term.** The 11 continuing organisations are doubly selected survivors with no comparison group. Their estimate is likely optimistic. But an uncontrolled before–after change can be biased in either direction, for example by economic conditions. So "likely optimistic" is accurate and "upper bound" is not.
- **Hours baseline.** The 40.3-hour baseline is the figure Varga & Holm reported for all 27 time-tracking organisations. Confirm that all 11 continuers track time, and use their own baseline.
- **Non-response.** 9 of the 23 organisations with records did not respond. Non-respondents may include further reverters.
- **"All with client-facing or coverage obligations" glosses over one case.** The marketing agency cited client deadlines. Under the meta-analysis's coding, marketing counts as discretionary work, and its "output can be produced at any time within a deadline" definition fits deadline-driven work. A discretionary organisation reverting is informative. Deadline clustering may limit the reduced-hours model even outside coverage-bound work, so it shouldn't be folded into the coverage story.

## Section 5: responses to earlier claims

- **Against Varga & Holm.** Fair for the discretionary, public-sector case-processing setting. The gain survives the measures they recommended, subject to issue 1 above. Two qualifications:
  - The counter arm ended at month 12, so "analysis of all enrolled units" at 24 months isn't met.
  - The rebuttal of the month-ten claim is partly aimed at a weaker version than Varga & Holm made. They extrapolated self-reported energy and argued the residual gain wouldn't last. They did not forecast per-hour output reaching zero at month ten.
- **Against the meta-analysis.** Persuasive and important. All four long-follow-up studies being uncontrolled and using scheduled hours is exactly the confound that point should have checked. But the alternative evidence offered is a single study whose decline is untested and possibly contaminated (issues 2 and 3).

## Still unaddressed from earlier rounds

- **Inference with few clusters.** The method behind the 7-v-7 confidence intervals is still not stated. Randomisation inference or a wild cluster bootstrap would be more credible.
- **Sick days.** The −27% may still be partly mechanical if schedules involve fewer working days. Report absence as a share of scheduled hours.
- **Quality and resignations.** Both are still raw comparisons without confidence intervals.
- **Authorship.** The authors are evaluating their own trial and defending their own hypothesis, and Okafor is a Halden author. That isn't a problem in itself, but independent replication of the mediation result matters more as a result.

## Overall

The defensible headline is this. In public-sector case processing, randomised evidence with record-based output finds a per-hour gain of roughly 8–10% at two years, with output per worker slightly below control. Counter work failed clearly. Fewer meetings are a plausible major contributor.

That holds only if log hours are what the paper says. Pinning down the log-time definition and correcting for the meeting-audit contamination would show whether "8.5%" and "47%" stand.
